content.title: Fixing Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers
content.overview: This lesson focuses on ensuring that modifying phrases are placed correctly next to the nouns they describe. On the ACT, sentences often contain 'dangling' or 'misplaced' modifiers that create illogical or confusing meanings by describing the wrong subject.
learning_objectives: Identify modifying phrases that lack a clear or adjacent actor.
Apply the 'Attach the Actor' strategy to fix dangling modifiers.
Distinguish between active and passive voice to ensure the actor is the subject of the sentence.
Verify that a modifier logically describes the noun immediately following it.

sections.title: Understanding Modifiers and Actors
sections.content: A modifier is a word or phrase that provides extra information about another part of the sentence. Often, these are participial phrases starting with '-ing' (e.g., 'Walking to school') or '-ed' (e.g., 'Exhausted by the heat'). The 'actor' is the person or thing that the modifier is meant to describe. For a sentence to be grammatically correct and logical, the actor must be placed immediately next to the modifier.

sections.title: Dangling vs. Misplaced Modifiers
sections.content: A dangling modifier occurs when the intended actor is missing from the sentence entirely or is not the subject of the main clause. A misplaced modifier occurs when the modifier is physically separated from the noun it describes, often appearing to describe a different noun instead. On the ACT, these errors usually appear at the beginning of a sentence: [Modifying Phrase], [Subject] [Verb]...

sections.title: The Attach the Actor Strategy
sections.content: To fix these errors, follow three steps: 1. Identify the modifier and determine who or what is actually performing that action (the actor). 2. Rewrite the sentence so the actor immediately follows the comma after the introductory modifier. 3. Use an active verb to ensure the actor is the one performing the action, rather than being acted upon (passive voice).

worked_examples.question: Identify the error and correct: 'Covered in thick mud, the hose was used by the gardener to clean the truck.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the modifier: 'Covered in thick mud.' 2. Identify the intended actor: The truck (or possibly the gardener, but contextually the truck is being cleaned). 3. Check the current subject: 'the hose.' This implies the hose is covered in mud, which is illogical. 4. Rewrite: 'Covered in thick mud, the truck was cleaned by the gardener with a hose.' OR 'To clean the truck covered in thick mud, the gardener used a hose.'

worked_examples.question:
Choose the best revision: 'While eating lunch, the phone rang constantly.'
A. NO CHANGE
B. While eating lunch, the phone was ringing.
C. While eating lunch, Sarah heard the phone ring constantly.
D. While eating lunch, the ringing phone was heard by Sarah.
worked_examples.solution: 1. The modifier is 'While eating lunch.' 2. The actor must be a person (Sarah), not 'the phone.' 3. Choice C places 'Sarah' immediately after the modifier and uses an active verb ('heard'). Choice D uses passive voice and places 'the ringing phone' next to the modifier, which is incorrect. Correct answer: C.

common_mistakes: Assuming the sentence is correct because the meaning is 'obvious' despite the grammar (e.g., knowing a person is eating even if the sentence says the phone is eating).
Choosing a passive voice revision that still leaves the wrong noun next to the modifier.
Failing to realize that the noun immediately following an introductory phrase is the one being modified.
exam_tips: When you see an '-ing' phrase at the start of a sentence, immediately look at the noun after the comma.
If the noun after the comma cannot logically perform the action in the introductory phrase, the sentence has a dangling modifier.
The ACT prefers active voice (Subject-Verb-Object) because it usually places the actor in the correct position.
content.recap: To fix dangling or misplaced modifiers, identify the intended actor and place it immediately after the modifying phrase. Ensure the sentence uses an active structure so the modifier logically describes the subject.

knowledge_claims.content: A modifier is a phrase, often starting with an '-ing' or '-ed' verb, that provides additional information about a noun.
The 'actor' is the specific person or thing that a modifying phrase is intended to describe.
In standard English, an introductory modifying phrase must be immediately followed by the noun it describes.
A dangling modifier is recognized when the intended actor is either missing from the sentence or is not the subject of the main clause.
A misplaced modifier is recognized when a modifier is positioned next to a noun it is not intended to describe, creating an illogical meaning.
The first step in the 'Attach the Actor' strategy is to identify the modifying phrase and underline the noun it should logically describe.
To correct a dangling modifier, rewrite the sentence so the actor immediately follows the modifier, typically after a comma.
Active voice is generally preferred over passive voice in modifier corrections because it keeps the actor as the clear subject performing the action.
A final check for modifier errors involves reading the sentence aloud to ensure the modifier logically and directly describes the noun that follows it.
A common mistake is choosing a revision that keeps the modifier next to the wrong noun simply because the overall meaning of the sentence seems clear.
If a sentence begins with 'Running quickly,' the noun immediately following the comma must be the entity that is actually running.
In the sentence 'Sizzling on the grill, the chef flipped the burgers,' the modifier 'Sizzling on the grill' incorrectly describes 'the chef' instead of 'the burgers.'

items.stem:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 1: The Clock Above Alder Street
[1] After three months of fundraising [[a neighborhood restoration crew began]] to repair the brass clock above Alder Street Market. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a market hall built in 1911, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] wear marks showed that an earlier repairer had reversed two nearly identical wheels. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because replacement parts would have erased those clues. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the crew cleaned and reused the original wheels. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the clock kept accurate time through a week of rain. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.]]

Which replacement for the wording marked [3] avoids a misplaced modifier?

options.A: the first set of observations was recorded by the team
options.B: the observations, which were first, were recorded
options.C: the team recorded its first set of observations
options.D: there was a first set of observations recorded

items.explanation: The noun immediately after the introductory modifier must be the actor using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears; 'a neighborhood restoration crew' is that actor.

items.stem:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 2: Counting After Dark
[1] After several cloudy evenings [[a coastal ecology class began]] to count juvenile crabs in tide pools after sunset. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a protected inlet beside the school, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] the smallest crabs appeared most often under flat stones near eelgrass. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because bright white light changed the animals’ movement. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the class switched to dim red lamps and repeated the first survey. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the second set of counts was more consistent. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the revised method gave park staff a dependable baseline for future surveys.]]

Which replacement for the wording marked [3] avoids a misplaced modifier?

options.A: the team recorded its first set of observations
options.B: the first set of observations was recorded by the team
options.C: the observations, which were first, were recorded
options.D: there was a first set of observations recorded

items.explanation: The noun immediately after the introductory modifier must be the actor using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets; 'a coastal ecology class' is that actor.

videoLesson.title: Revise Dangling Modifiers to Name Actor
videoLesson.description: Identify modifiers missing a clear actor and the noun they should modify. Underline that noun and rewrite so the actor immediately follows the modifier with an active verb.
